gabarito.reason:
The first finding is a real weakness. In HashUtils.deriveKey the user's shared "Salt" string is really the password: it is passed as the PBEKeySpec password, and the PBKDF2 salt is BuildConfig.APP_SALT + that same password. APP_SALT is built into the APK and defaults to the public value "Salty@AES-256" in app/build.gradle. So the salt is fixed and can be computed from the password; it is not random. An attacker can therefore build one dictionary of PBKDF2-SHA256 outputs (600k iterations) that works against every message made by every install of the official build. The salt does nothing to make each message different, and user-chosen shared keys are likely to be weak. The second finding (CipherSpec in encode) only follows from the first: the key passed to Cipher.init was derived from that PBEKeySpec. AES-GCM with a fresh 12-byte IV from SecureRandom and a 128-bit tag is fine and is not a separate problem. A fix is not a one-line change. The encoded string Base64(iv || ciphertext) is a format that users exchange between installs (the README describes swapping encrypted messages using a shared Salt). It is also stored in the Room history (MessageEntry.encodedMessage). The format has no salt field, which is why the salt is deterministic today. A fix has to generate a random salt (16+ bytes from SecureRandom) for each message, put it in the output with a version marker, and keep decoding the old format. Older app versions still could not read new messages. A careful contributor could send that PR, or could open an ISSUE that explains the precomputation risk and the compatibility cost and leaves the format decision to the maintainers. NO_ACTION is not appropriate: the salt really is fixed and public in the default build, and the report correctly points to it.

Second judge: The finding identifies a real KDF weakness. deriveKey uses the user-entered shared secret as the PBKDF2 password and APP_SALT concatenated with that same secret as its salt. APP_SALT defaults to "Salty@AES-256" and can be overridden at build time; neither source supplies an independent random KDF salt. Reusing a password therefore reuses its derived key across messages and compatible installations, allowing password-guessing work to be amortized. The CipherSpec finding propagates that upstream finding; it does not identify a separate cipher configuration defect. encode already generates a fresh 12-byte SecureRandom GCM IV and uses a 128-bit authentication tag. An issue explaining this and the compatibility implications is acceptable, as is a complete PR. Simply inserting randomness into deriveKey would break decryption: ciphertext currently contains only Base64(IV || ciphertext || tag), is copied to recipients, and is saved in Room history.
must_change: deriveKey must use a salt of at least 16 bytes, freshly generated with SecureRandom for each encode, instead of APP_SALT + the user's password; the password itself stays the user's shared key
encode must put the random salt in its output (e.g. version/marker byte || salt || 12-byte IV || ciphertext+tag, Base64 NO_WRAP) so the receiver can read it and derive the same key
decode must read the salt from the new format and derive the key with it, telling the new format apart from the old one by an explicit version/marker rather than by guessing
isValidEncodedMessage and the length checks in decode must account for the longer new format (salt + IV + tag)

For new encryptions, derive the key using an independent cryptographically random KDF salt, while retaining the user-entered shared secret as the password. Randomizing APP_SALT at build time is insufficient.

Carry the KDF salt in the copied/stored message envelope and have decode extract and reuse it. Introduce an identifiable format/version, validate its structure, and update both encoding and decoding; do not regenerate the salt during decryption or keep it only on the sender's device.
Provide a legacy decoding path and verify legacy compatibility, new-format round trips across independent instances, randomized salt generation, and rejection of wrong passwords or tampered messages.
must_not_break: Decoding of existing messages in the old Base64(iv || ciphertext) format, created with the deterministic APP_SALT+password salt, both those pasted from other users on older app versions and those stored in the Room history (MessageEntry.encodedMessage); the old derivation path must stay available for decode
The APP_SALT build-time configuration (env var with default "Salty@AES-256"): builds that set a custom APP_SALT must still decode their own old messages
Two installs of the new version must still exchange messages using only the shared Salt string, with no extra secret or key exchange
AES-256-GCM with a 12-byte random IV per message, a 128-bit tag, PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256 with 600,000 iterations, and a 256-bit key, as the README advertises; must not be weakened
Room database schema version 2 and the stored MessageEntry fields, with no destructive migration of history
minSdk 24 support (no APIs that need a higher SDK level than the current code uses)
Error handling in SaltyViewModel: a wrong key or corrupted message must still surface as DecodingException / 'Wrong key or corrupted message', not crash

Existing saved and previously copied ciphertext must remain decryptable with the original shared secret and matching APP_SALT. Legacy decoding must preserve PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256, 600000 iterations, 256-bit output, the exact UTF-8 APP_SALT-plus-password salt construction, and the existing 12-byte-IV AES-GCM layout.

Preserve cross-device exchange using only the encoded text and shared secret. A new format requires an explicit peer compatibility transition; unchanged releases cannot decode it automatically. Do not silently replace the shared-secret scheme with device-bound keys or local-only salt storage.

Preserve Room history and its copy workflows without destructive migration. History contains the original message, encoded message, and shared secret; fixing this report must not discard those records.

Preserve authenticated encryption, fresh GCM IVs, strong derivation parameters, UTF-8 message handling, and failure on authentication errors. Do not remove authentication or weaken cryptography to silence the checker.
Account for both default and custom APP_SALT builds, and retain the declared Android minSdk 24 support when choosing implementation APIs or dependencies.
gabarito.fixed_by: reading v2, the author's rule of 2026-11-14 (build_gabarito_v2.py)

cards.notes: New messages get a 16-byte SecureRandom salt behind an unambiguous 'salty:v2:' prefix. The legacy APP_SALT+password path and the length checks are handled correctly. No tests are in the diff, and new messages no longer mix in APP_SALT.

Random 16-byte salt under a 'v2:' prefix, with APP_SALT appended to the password. The legacy derivation is kept exactly. The fallback to legacy after a v2 failure is unnecessary but harmless, and there are no tests.

Accurately explains the fixed salt built from APP_SALT plus the password, why precomputation works, the format and compatibility tradeoffs, and that the CipherSpec finding follows from the first. A good reason to defer the decision to the maintainers.

A clean versioned format (APP_SALT plus a random salt) with a correct legacy path and thorough Robolectric tests. The card says the author did not build this diff, yet the text claims the APK build and all tests passed, and it leaks a local build_check path.

Accurate and specific about the deterministic salt, the public default APP_SALT, and the CipherSpec finding being the same issue. It also covers format compatibility and the Room history. The suggested fallback on tag failure has no marker, but that is acceptable in an issue.

A 6-byte in-band marker plus a random salt, a length-delimited password that includes APP_SALT, and a legacy fallback on tag failure, which is fine given the 2^-48 marker collision chance. The description leaves out that older app versions cannot read new messages, and there are no tests.

Correct '=v2:' format with a random salt and a separate legacy derivation. The hand-rolled findV2PayloadStart parser is convoluted, and a reviewer would ask for it to be simplified. The description does not say that old app versions cannot read new messages.

Clean 'SALTY2:'-prefixed format with a random salt and a legacy path that keeps the exact old derivation, plus updated length checks. There are no tests. The terse description does not say that APP_SALT no longer affects new messages or describe the format.
A well-structured 'salty:v1:' format with a legacy path and fixture-based tests. The card says the author did not build this diff, but the text claims the debug build and all eight tests passed.

Correctly describes the salt as a pure function of the password, the precomputation risk, and that a version marker plus legacy fallback is needed for history and shared messages. Leaves the choice to the maintainers.

Uses an '=Salty2:' prefix (legacy Base64 never starts with '=') and a random salt, with APP_SALT moved into the GCM AAD. The legacy path is preserved. There are no tests, and the new-format length check ignores the tag, which is minor. The text honestly says tests were not run.

The HashUtils change is correct: a 'salty:v1:' prefix, a random salt and a legacy path. The test setup uses the deprecated android.test InstrumentationTestRunner and would need rework. The text claims the debug build passed, but the card says the author did not build this diff.

The new salt is 16 random bytes plus APP_SALT plus the password, under a 'SALTY2:' prefix, and the legacy path is preserved. Falling back to legacy after a prefixed decode fails is redundant but harmless, and there are no tests.
An in-band 9-byte marker, a random salt, and a password that includes APP_SALT, with a legacy fallback. Correct overall. isValidEncodedMessage was not updated (it is unused) and there are no tests.

A well-structured 'salty:v2:' format with a correct legacy derivation, validation and good tests. The card says the author did not build this diff, but the text claims the debug build and all five tests passed.

Adds a random salt, but there is no version marker: decode guesses the format by trying the new layout and falling back to legacy when the tag check fails. That doubles the 600k-iteration PBKDF2 cost for legacy messages and wrong keys, and the explicit marker the fix needs is missing. The description is accurate and says this plainly.
An in-band 6-byte marker, with the salt built from APP_SALT, the password and 16 random bytes, and a legacy fallback. It works. The description is vague ('a random component') and there are no tests.

A random salt with APP_SALT moved into the AAD, but no format marker: it trial-decrypts the new layout and falls back to legacy, so legacy decodes run PBKDF2 twice. The text is thorough and honest about these tradeoffs.

A clean 'v2:' format and parser with the exact legacy derivation and comprehensive tests. The card says the author did not build this diff, but the text claims all seven tests passed and that build_check succeeded.

An 8-byte in-band marker and a random salt, with a legacy fallback on a GeneralSecurityException. The behaviour is correct, but there are no tests, and the brief description does not say that APP_SALT is dropped from new derivations.
An accurate analysis of the deterministic salt and the public default APP_SALT, with sensible questions on compatibility. It leaves out that older app versions could not decode new messages.
Wrongly concludes there is no security impact. The fixed, public, password-derived salt lets attackers reuse precomputation across all messages and installs.
